name: When to Cut Losses
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Discipline of Walking Away
lesson.summary: Deciding when to stop funding a struggling quantum computing bet requires separating sunk costs from forward looking judgment, using the same expected value thinking that makes venture capital's overall loss rates survivable.
lesson.body:
The sunk cost trap is the well known bias where people let money, time, or effort already spent influence a decision about what to do next, even though none of it can be recovered regardless of the choice made going forward. A rational decision about whether to keep funding a struggling quantum company should rest entirely on the future: the probability of eventual success from this point on, the additional capital and time required to get there, and what else that capital and time could accomplish if redirected elsewhere. The 50 million already invested is gone either way and should not appear anywhere in the forward looking calculation, yet in practice it is often the single biggest reason investors and founders keep funding a company the evidence says will not work out.

Venture Capital Loss Rates supplies the discipline that makes walking away rational rather than defeatist. Because the venture model expects most bets to fail while a few winners carry the fund, an investor's job is to keep reassessing, with fresh eyes, whether each company still belongs among the few worth continued funding. An investor who cannot write off a losing position because it feels like admitting a mistake is substituting ego protection for portfolio math, and every extra dollar poured into a low probability company is a dollar unavailable for a higher probability one.

Expected value makes this concrete: multiply each outcome's payoff by its probability and sum. Suppose a struggling company needs 20 million more to reach its next milestone, at which point investors estimate a 15 percent chance it becomes worth 500 million and an 85 percent chance it is worth near zero. Expected value is 0.15 times 500 million plus 0.85 times 0, which is 75 million, comfortably above the 20 million cost, so the bet is still worth making. If the probability of success has instead fallen to 2 percent, expected value becomes 0.02 times 500 million, or 10 million, below the 20 million cost, and the rational move flips to walking away, regardless of what came before.

This is uncomfortable in practice because quantum computing genuinely rewards patience: the underlying physics and engineering take real time to mature, and a company that looks stalled at year five might still be on a legitimate multi decade path, as the technology readiness concepts ahead will make precise. The skill being described here is not blanket cynicism toward every struggling company, it is the discipline of updating the probability estimate honestly as new evidence arrives, rather than anchoring to the story told at the initial investment, and acting on that updated estimate even when a large sunk cost makes acting on it feel painful.

Judging whether a struggling technology deserves continued patience needs an objective yardstick for maturity, separate from how exciting the pitch sounds. That yardstick is introduced next.
